summary: Describes a situation in which the Border Gateway Protocol (BGP), the routing protocol between autonomous systems, can fall into a persistent route oscillation that never settles. It explains the conditions that cause this behavior.

plainLanguage.summary: Imagine two people who keep changing their minds because of what the other chose, so neither ever settles. This document explains how internet routers can get stuck in that loop.

questions: what is bgp persistent route oscillation
why do bgp routes keep flapping
what is type i churn in bgp
how to avoid bgp med oscillation
subtitle: How BGP route reflectors and confederations, combined with MED, can make routers flip best paths forever.

tldr.problem: BGP's scaling tools, route reflection and AS confederations, hide some exit points from some routers, and with MED comparisons this partial view can make best-path choices chase each other without end.
tldr.mechanism: The memo defines two kinds of persistent oscillation, Type I and Type II, walks through step-by-step examples of each, and lists network design workarounds.
tldr.outcome: The cycles are deterministic and can be avoided by design choices, but the authors say protocol enhancements are needed because such design rules are an unreasonable long-term solution.

today: RFC 3345 is an Informational memo, and the unit metadata shows it has not been obsoleted or updated. It records the problem as understood in August 2002 and calls for protocol enhancements.

sections.title: The Problem
sections.content:
BGP is the routing protocol between autonomous systems, and its main job is to exchange network reachability information. In some configurations, the two scaling mechanisms for internal BGP (iBGP), route reflection (RFC 2796) and AS confederations (RFC 3065), cause persistent route oscillation.

The trigger is the MULTI_EXIT_DISC (MED) attribute, which BGP-4 says is comparable only between routes learned from the same neighboring AS. In a full iBGP mesh every router sees all exit points, so this is harmless. Reflectors and confederations remove the full mesh, so a router may see only some exit points. Its best-path decision can then be inconsistent with others, and if the inconsistency spans several peering routers the result is a loop.

The behavior is deterministic and avoidable with rudimentary design principles. The authors want to raise operator awareness and prompt protocol proposals. They classify the cases as Type I and Type II.
sections.plainLanguage: When a big network is split into smaller groups to keep it manageable, each router sees only part of the picture. Different partial pictures can make routers disagree forever.

sections.title: Type I Churn
sections.content:
Type I churn occurs only when both conditions hold: a single-level route reflection or confederation design is used, and the network accepts MED from two or more ASs for one prefix with unique MED values. The memo also notes that non-deterministic ordering of paths can cause oscillation, and that most vendors default to deterministic ordering or provide a knob for it.

The reflection example has AS1 with two clusters. Reflector Ra has clients Rb and Rc, and reflector Rd has client Re. The prefix is 10.0.0.0/8, reachable via AS10 (MED 10), and AS6 (MED 1 at Rc, MED 0 at Re). Ra picks a path, advertises it, Rd then prefers a path by lower MED, Ra then prefers a different path by lower IGP metric, Rd changes again, and Ra is back at its starting table. The cycle repeats.

The confederation example follows the same pattern with Sub-ASs 65000 and 65001. There the memo adds that Ra does not compute the best path for a prefix unless its best route was withdrawn, until its periodic BGP scanner runs.
sections.plainLanguage: Two bosses each pick a favorite based on what the other one picked last. Each pick changes the other boss's mind, so they go round and round.

sections.title: Type II Churn
sections.content:
Type II churn needs more than one tier of route reflection or Sub-ASs, plus MED accepted from two or more ASs with unique values. The memo shows it with confederations only, to keep things short.

In the example AS 1 has Sub-ASs 65500, 65501 and 65502, and prefix 10.0.0.0/8 is reachable through AS 200 and AS 300, both transiting AS 400. Re first picks the path via AS 200 on IGP metric, because MEDs from different ASs are not compared. After Rd and Rc exchange routes, a lower MED wins at Rd, then Re prefers the AS 300 path on IGP metric, and so on until the tables return to the second step and loop. The memo traces eight steps.
sections.plainLanguage: With more layers of groups, the routers can again keep switching favorites, because each layer sees a different slice of the choices.

sections.title: Workarounds
sections.content:
For Type I with route reflection, make inter-cluster links have a higher IGP metric than intra-cluster links. This is the preferred choice. With confederations, do the same for inter-Sub-AS versus intra-Sub-AS links.

Other options apply to both types:

  • Do not accept MEDs from peers, which may not be feasible.
  • Use attributes higher in the decision process so the MED step is not reached. For Type II, local-pref set per advertising AS would do this.
  • Always compare MEDs across ASs. The memo calls this probably a bad idea because it mostly defeats the purpose of MEDs.
  • Use a full iBGP mesh, which is not feasible for ASs with many BGP speakers.

For Type II, do not use more than one tier of reflection or Sub-ASs, or mesh the clients (for confederations, mesh the border routers at each level). The memo says it knows of no large provider doing the per-prefix policies that the local-pref workaround needs.
sections.plainLanguage: The fixes are to make the routers stop caring about the confusing tie-breaker, make short hops cheaper than long hops, or let every router see everything.

sections.title: Future Work and Security
sections.content:
The authors state that protocol enhancements must be pursued. Imposing network design requirements like those above is clearly an unreasonable long-term solution, and problems like this should not occur under default protocol configurations.

The Security Considerations section says the discussion introduces no new security concerns to BGP or to the specifications it references.
sections.plainLanguage: The authors say people should not have to work around this forever. The protocol itself should be fixed. They do not see any new safety risks.
